NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday launched the 'Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan', calling on the country's youth to stay physically and mentally fit and remain away from drug abuse.He said achieving the goal of a developed India requires a healthy, confident and drug-free younger generation. During his address, PM Modi also highlighed how the drugs affect one's family and career.Launching the campaign through video conferencing, PM Modi said the initiative is not only for individuals, families and society but also for the nation. He added that the next 100 Sundays would represent 100 strong steps towards a drug-free India."Next 100 Sundays will mark 100 strong steps towards drug-free India," he said.PM Modi also warned that drug trafficking was part of a larger strategy by hostile forces to weaken India and called for greater public vigilance. "Hurting India's interests by supplying drugs part of enemy nations' terror plan," he said.The 'Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan' aims to encourage young people to stay away from substance abuse and become ambassadors of positive social change in their communities.The launch marks the beginning of a 100-week nationwide Jan Bhagidari campaign, under which awareness programmes will be organised every Sunday across the country.Activities will include sports events, walkathons, meditation sessions, cultural programmes, street plays, discussions, art competitions and community engagement initiatives.The campaign brings together educational institutions, youth organisations, civil society groups, industry bodies and more than 125 spiritual organisations to build a collective movement against substance abuse.Youth from over 10,000 locations across the country are participating through schools, colleges, universities, MY Bharat volunteers, NSS volunteers, youth clubs, NGOs and industry associations.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the 'Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan' The campaign aims to encourage young people to become ambassadors of positive social change in their communities. PM Modi also warned that drug trafficking was part of a larger strategy by hostile forces to weaken India.

Article Title: 'Dismantle terror infrastructure first': India's US envoy hits out at Pakistan over Indus Waters Treaty
Article Text:

India’s envoy to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra said Pakistan had eroded the foundation of the Indus Waters Treaty over the past five decades. He added that Islamabad had “dismantled” the goodwill and friendship that underpinned the 1960 agreement, and that New Delhi’s decision to keep the treaty in abeyance merely acknowledged that reality.As reported by US' Newsweek magazine, Kwatra said the treaty’s preamble reflected a commitment made 'in a spirit of goodwill and friendship', but Pakistan’s conduct had weakened that foundation over half a century.“It is worth remembering that the treaty's preamble declares it was concluded ‘in a spirit of goodwill and friendship’. Pakistan spent half a century dismantling that goodwill and friendship. The abeyance merely acknowledges what Pakistan's conduct had already destroyed,” Kwatra said.His remarks came after Pakistan recently hosted a conference protesting India’s decision to keep the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance on April 23 last year, a day after Pakistan-trained terrorists killed 26 people in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir.The IWT, signed by India and Pakistan in 1960, divided the waters of the six rivers of the Indus basin between the two countries. India was given control over the eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej which account for about 20 per cent of the basin’s water, while Pakistan received rights over the western rivers Indus, Jhelum and Chenab carrying around 80 per cent.“That asymmetry stifled development for decades in Indian regions that could have benefited from better water rights. India honoured the treaty anyway,” Kwatra said according to Newsweek.The envoy said Pakistan’s approach towards India had been marked by wars, hostility and cross-border terrorism, citing the 1965, 1971 and 1999 conflicts along with major terror attacks, including the 2001 Parliament attack, the 2008 Mumbai attacks, the 2016 Uri and Pathankot attacks, the 2019 Pulwama attack and the 2025 Pahalgam attack.Kwatra also said that if Pakistan sincerely wanted India’s cooperation on bilateral issues, it must first dismantle the terror infrastructure it has built over the years.On implementation of the treaty, Kwatra alleged that Pakistan had repeatedly delayed Indian projects and opposed efforts to revisit the agreement in view of changing technology and requirements.“Pakistan also consistently blocked India's initiatives to renegotiate the treaty in light of six decades of technological change, which would have let India develop its hydropower potential,” Kwatra added.“Bit by bit, Pakistan eroded India's faith that it could exercise its rights under the treaty, or hope for a better one suited to today's realities,” he said.Responding to calls for India and Pakistan to resume talks, Kwatra said past initiatives had failed to address core concerns.“Prime Minister Narendra Modi has clearly voiced India’s stand today: ‘Terror and talks cannot go together... Terror and trade cannot go together... Water and blood cannot flow together',” Kwatra said.Kwatra also said Pakistan should focus on improving its own water management instead of blaming India for its challenges."The Government of Pakistan would do better to fix its dismal water productivity, than to stage conferences blaming India and issuing threats,” he said, adding, “The habit of pinning every domestic failure on India has grown old."
Article Summary: India’s envoy to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra said Pakistan had eroded the foundation of the Indus Waters Treaty over the past five decades. He added that Islamabad had ‘dismantled’ the goodwill and friendship that underpinned the 1960 agreement. The IWT, signed by India and Pakistan in 1960, divided the waters of the six rivers of theindus basin.

NEW DELHI: Want to age more slowly? The answer may lie not just in exercise and diet, but also in a trip to the theatre, museum or even the cinema.A new study by Japanese researchers has found that older adults who engage more frequently in cultural activities tend to have a lower physiological age—a measure of how well the body's organs and systems are functioning—than their actual age, suggesting cultural engagement may be an overlooked tool for healthy ageing.Researchers from the Institute of Science Tokyo analysed 4,207 observations from 1,899 adults aged 50 years and above in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. Participants who more frequently visited cinemas, museums, art galleries, theatres, concerts or the opera had lower physiological age. Every one-point increase in cultural engagement score was associated with a 0.085-year reduction in physiological age, even after adjusting for income, health status, employment, smoking, physical activity and other factors. The association persisted in a four-year follow-up analysis. Physiological age, estimated using 10 markers including blood pressure, lung function, grip strength, walking speed, BMI, haemoglobin, cholesterol and blood sugar, is considered a better predictor of disease and mortality than chronological age.The researchers said cultural engagement may promote healthy ageing by strengthening social connections, reducing loneliness and stress, improving mental well-being and encouraging healthier lifestyles.Indian experts said the findings reinforce the importance of staying socially engaged as people age.Dr Prasun Chatterjee, Group Clinical Lead, Department of Geriatric Medicine and Longevity Sciences, Apollo Hospitals, and former professor at AIIMS, said the findings reinforce that healthy ageing depends not only on diet and exercise but also on social and cultural engagement. Social interaction improves memory and mood by boosting serotonin and dopamine, enhancing emotional well-being, memory and a sense of purpose, which encourage healthier lifestyles. Article Title: Global breastfeeding rates rise, India yet to arrest decline
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Even as exclusive breastfeeding rates have improved globally over the past decade, India continues to lag behind, with the proportion of infants exclusively breastfed for the first six months declining from 63.7% in NFHS-5 (2019-21) to 55.8% in NFHS-6 (2023-24).Ahead of World Breastfeeding Week (August 1-7), the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF called for stronger support systems for mothers, saying global exclusive breastfeeding has increased from about 37% in 2012 to over 47% today, driven by sustained investments in health systems, community counselling and maternity protection. However, the agencies said progress remains uneven and many countries continue to fall short of global targets.Responding to a question in the Rajya Sabha, the Union health ministry attributed the decline in India's exclusive breastfeeding rate to multiple factors, including socio-cultural practices, family customs, individual preferences, the use of pre-lacteal feeds and infant milk substitutes, and breastfeeding frequency.The ministry, however, highlighted improvements in other breastfeeding indicators.Early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour of birth increased from 41.8% to 50.1%, while the proportion of infants below six months receiving any breast milk rose marginally from 95.1% to 95.6%.The Rajya Sabha question had sought to know whether the government had assessed the impact of rising Caesarean deliveries, inadequate postnatal lactation counselling and early return to work, particularly among women in the informal sector. While the ministry did not provide findings of any such assessment, it said the National Health Mission promotes exclusive breastfeeding through the Mother Absolute Affection (MAA) programme, lactation management centres, healthcare worker training, Poshan Tracker-based counselling and community awareness campaigns.It also cited a 2025 NITI Aayog evaluation, which found that new mothers were receiving information on exclusive breastfeeding during the postnatal period.Calling breastfeeding one of the most effective public health interventions, WHO and UNICEF said it provides essential nutrition, protects children against infections, strengthens immunity, supports cognitive development and lowers mothers' risk of breast and ovarian cancers and type 2 diabetes. The agencies said scaling up proven interventions, including skilled breastfeeding support, community counselling, paid maternity leave, supportive workplace policies and stronger regulation of breast-milk substitute marketing, could prevent nearly 400,000 child deaths and 140,000 maternal deaths globally every year.
Article Summary: The proportion of infants exclusively breastfed for the first six months has declined from 63.7% in 2019-21 to 55.8% in 2023-24. The Union health ministry attributed the decline in India's exclusive breastfeeding rate to multiple factors.

NEW DELHI: Long and crushing working hours have become a serious challenge for resident doctors, causing them psychological distress and mental health problems. Flagging the issue in an affidavit before Supreme Court, National Medical Commission (NMC) has stressed that reasonable working hours and time for rest are a must for their wellbeing and proper functioning, as well as proper patient care. It, however, expressed its inability to ensure the same, saying the matter falls within the domain of central and state health authorities.In the affidavit filed in response to a PIL by a group of doctors seeking healthy working conditions, the commission placed the findings of its task force, which had projected a grim picture of what doctors have to endure.“The demanding schedules, including long and multiple 24-hour duties (sometimes 3-5 consecutive duties), were significant stressors for most post graduate doctors. These extended hours without adequate rest led to physical and mental exhaustion, negatively impacting their performance and health,” commission said, referring to the report.Doctors’ organisation ‘United Doctors Front’ had approached the court demanding healthy working conditions, pointing out that cases of doctors’ suicides are on the rise and claiming that 150 such cases have been reported in five years.
Article Summary: Long and crushing working hours have become a serious challenge for resident doctors. NEW DELHI: A 52-year-old BSF constable who recently returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo as part of an Indian UN peacekeeping contingent has been admitted to the isolation ward at the Ebola Nursing Home of Dr Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital after developing fever during mandatory quarantine, triggering Ebola surveillance protocols.The constable, who arrived in India on July 11, had been under a 21-day quarantine at the Airport Health Organisation (APHO) facility following his return from Congo, an Ebola-endemic region. On the evening of 20th day of quarantine, he developed a fever along with body aches.As per protocol, he was shifted to the designated Ebola isolation facility at RML Hospital. His blood sample has been sent to the National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune, for confirmatory testing. The test report is awaited.Officials said the patient is being managed in strict isolation while health authorities continue to monitor the situation. At present, the case remains suspected, and Ebola infection has not been confirmed.India follows enhanced screening and quarantine measures for personnel returning from Ebola-affected regions. Suspected cases are isolated immediately and samples are tested at designated reference laboratories before a diagnosis is confirmed.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday inaugurated the Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport at Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh 's Vizianagaram district, a nearly Rs 5,000 crore project that the state government says will transform North Andhra into a major economic and industrial hub. Calling the airport a key milestone in the state's growth story, the PM said the NDA government was working at "double speed"for the state's development.During his address, the Prime Minister also took a veiled swipe at the Gandhi family, saying airports in the past were often named after "a single family". He said the NDA government had instead chosen to honour national icons by naming airports after figures such as Valmiki, Sant Ravidas and Alluri Sitarama Raju.The PM was accorded a grand ceremonial welcome, with around 13,500 tribal women performing the traditional Dhimsa dance. The airport premises were adorned with displays celebrating Andhra Pradesh's rich cultural heritage, including Etikoppaka artwork and motifs depicting the state's geographical identity.PM Modi was received by Andhra Pradesh chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu, deputy chief minister Pawan Kalyan, and union civil aviation minister K Ram Mohan Naidu.He later witnessed the Dhimsa performance before formally inaugurating the airport.Developed by the GMR Group, the airport has been named after freedom fighter Alluri Sitarama Raju. It has been designed to handle six million passengers annually in its first phase, with a long-term expansion plan to increase capacity to 40 million passengers a year. Commercial flight operations are scheduled to begin on August 17.Also Read: PM Modi inaugurates Rs 5,640-crore Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport in Andhra Pradesh — See pics The Andhra Pradesh government has projected the airport as a key catalyst for industrial growth, employment generation, exports, skill development and improved connectivity across North Andhra.Following the inauguration, chief minister Naidu felicitated PM Modi with a traditional shawl before he laid the foundation stone, inaugurated and dedicated multiple development projects worth over Rs 17,900 crore.While addressing a public gathering in Bhogapuram after the airport's inaugural ceremony, PM Modi said Andhra would emerge as a manufacturing hub under Naidu's leadership. He said the NDA government was working at "double speed" for the state's development, highlighted railway projects worth around Rs 1 lakh crore, noted that the number of airports in India had increased from 74 to 166 over the past 12 years.The Prime Minister also laid the foundation stone for Andhra Pradesh's first semiconductor manufacturing facility under the India Semiconductor Mission, which is expected to produce around 96 million semiconductor chips annually. In addition, he launched power transmission projects worth over Rs 9,900 crore to strengthen the National Grid and facilitate renewable energy integration from Kurnool and Ananthapuram.He further dedicated to the nation and laid the foundation stone for National Highway projects worth over Rs 1,880 crore, including stretches of NH-365BG, the Tadipatri Bypass on NH-67, and a high-level bridge at Lingasamudram on NH-565. According to the government, these projects will improve regional connectivity, reduce travel time between Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad, ease congestion and enhance road safety.

Article Title: Tahir Hussain gets life for IB staffer’s killing in 2020 riots
Article Text:

Only death sentence will be justice’

NEW DELHI: Bringing the six-year-long trial in the murder of Intelligence Bureau staffer Ankit Sharma to a close, a Delhi court on Friday sentenced former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain and four others to life imprisonment, holding that Sharma was lynched “solely on account of his religion” during the 2020 northeast Delhi riots.Additional sessions judge Parveen Kumar Singh, however, declined the prosecution’s plea for the death penalty, ruling that while the brutality of the crime was undeniable, the prosecution had failed to prove any specific act committed by each convict during the murder.Pronouncing the sentence, Singh described the murder as one of exceptional brutality committed during the “communal violence that erupted in the wake of the protests against CAA/NRC”.The court held that the prosecution failed to prove allegations that Hussain had “aided, abetted, instigated or led the unlawful assembly”. Singh rejected the other convicts’ pleas that they were sole breadwinners. However, he did consider their educational background as a mitigating factor.On July 13, the court had convicted Hussain and four others, holding that the five were part of “a large crowd which, with animus against Hindus, had assembled...with a common object to commit rioting, loot, arson and to cause damage to the property and person of members of the Hindu community”, before murdering the IB staffer on Feb 25, 2020, whose body was later recovered from a drain.Hussain was sentenced to six months’ RI under IPC Section 188, three years under Section 153A, two years under Section 147, three years under Section 148, seven years under Section 365 and imprisonment for life under Section 302. All sentences will run concurrently. He was also fined Rs 1,000 under Section 188, Rs 20,000 each under Sections 153A, 147 and 148, Rs 50,000 under Section 365 and Rs 5 lakh under Section 302, with default sentences in case of non-payment.“The manner in which it was committed was of the utmost brutality. The victim was sucked in by the murderous mob, baying for blood... The assault was so fierce, unrelenting, and from such close quarters that even in death, the body did not immediately slump to the ground,” the judge held.The court noted that the violence did not end with Sharma’s death. His body, it observed, was strapped “like an animal”, dragged to Chand Bagh pulia and thrown into a drain. Calling it an “aggravating circumstance of immense magnitude”, the judge remarked, “As if the hatred had still not been satiated, the dead body was thereafter thrown into the nala. Therefore, the barbarity with which this horrendous murder was committed is nauseatingly sickening. ”Saying the “crime test” tilted the case towards the “rarest of rare” category, the judge weighed aggravating and mitigating circumst-ances before declining the capital punishment sought by special public prosecutor Madhukar Pandey, who maintained that the offence was part of “well-orchestrated communal violence” rather than a crime committed und-er sudden provocation.The court zoomed in on what it found to be the prosecution’s principal shortcoming — the lack of specificity regarding the individual role of each convict. Observing that “before a life is ordered to be extinguished by a judicial decree”, something more than mere membership of an unlawful assembly had to be proved, the judge held that the prosecution had failed to bridge that gap. While acknowledging the state’s contention that the use of a heavy cutting weapon reflected pre-planned and cold-blooded intent, the court said the time for drawing such inferences was long past and treated the lack of specificity as a “huge mitigation. ”Judge Singh rejected the convicts’ pleas that they were sole breadwinners and noted that the “monstrosity of the crime committed outweighs this mitigating circumstance”. At the same time, he found no material to conclude that they were beyond reform.It also noted that allegations of Hussain’s house being used as a “launchpad” for the riots were neither part of the charges framed nor specifically proved during trial. The judge also took note of the “entirely satisfactory” custodial conduct of Hussain, Kasim and Nazim, barring minor infractions by Kasim.Another mitigating factor, the court said, was the educational background of the convicts. It observed that “vested interests” had spread misinformation and whipped up a “religious frenzy”, making the uneducated co-convicts “more gullible and susceptible to such propaganda”, and held that this vulnerability to manipulation was relevant while determining the sentence.Hussain’s co-convicts were awarded life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC with a fine of Rs 25,000 each. They were also sentenced to six months under Section 188, three years under Section 153A, two years under Section 147, three years under Section 148 and seven years under Section 365 IPC, along with fines ranging from Rs 1,000 to Rs 10,000 under the respective provisions. All the sentences will run concurrently.As Hussain was being led out of the courtroom by police after the sentencing, he turned to those present and said, “High court se insaaf milega. Der aaye, lekin durust aaye.”Speaking to TOI, Ankur Sharma, brother of the IB staffer, said, “From day one, this has been a ‘rarest of rare’ case. While we appreciate that the trial court has delivered a conviction and handed down life imprisonment, true justice won’t be served until the perpetrators receive the death sentence, a demand we will aggressively pursue in the high court. The sheer brutality of the crime still haunts our family every single day; knowing he was inflicted with 51 wounds, subjected to acid, and dumped in a drain is a pain that never truly goes away. ”
Article Summary: Former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain and four others sentenced to life imprisonment. Sharma was lynched “solely on account of his religion’ during 2020 northeast Delhi riots. Prosecution failed to prove allegations that Hussain had “aided, abetted, instigated or led the unlawful assembly.

Article Title: India-China border trade resumes after 6 years
Article Text:

SHIMLA/PITHIRAGARH: India and China resumed traditional border trade Saturday through Lipulekh in Uttarakhand and Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh after nearly six years, restoring two key Himalayan trade routes that had remained closed since the Covid-19 pandemic.At Lipulekh in Uttarakhand's Pithoragarh district, the first batch of 16 traders and four support staff crossed into Tibet without goods as the two sides began restoring trade operations. Chinese authorities restricted the inaugural batch to 20 people, citing infrastructure constraints at the Taklakot trade mart and sought detailed personal information of all traders in advance. They also asked that priority be given to those who had participated in the last trading season in 2019.Accordingly, the traders' association selected traders whose goods had remained stranded at Taklakot after trade was suspended in 2020. "Priority was given to traders who had participated in the 2019 trading season and had left their goods at Taklakot," Dharchula SDM and district trade officer Ashish Joshi said.Meanwhile, in Himachal Pradesh, revenue minister Jagat Singh Negi flagged off the first batch of 16 Indian traders as they set off with their horses towards Shipki village in Tibet through the 3,930-metre-high Shipki La Pass.The trade, suspended since 2020 because of Covid, was scheduled to resume on June 1 but was delayed owing to security concerns and inadequate infrastructure at the trading post.Trade through Shipki La, which will remain open until Nov 30, will continue under the traditional barter system. Indian traders will be allowed to stay across the border for up to 72 hours, while the home department has cleared 53 traders after verification of their antecedents.Indian traders have been permitted to export 36 categories of goods, including dried fruits, spices, handicrafts and herbs, while Chinese traders can bring 20 categories of goods, including pashmina, wool, yak hair, sheepskin, goatskin and China clay. Officials said the overall list comprised 72 categories of tradable goods from the Indian side and 30 from the Chinese side.Negi also inaugurated the Rs 1.7 crore Chhuppan Trade Mart at Namgya village in Pooh subdivision near the international border to facilitate border trade.Replying to a demand by local traders to expand the list of tradable goods, Negi said the proposal would be placed before CM Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu and also with MEA.The routes were scheduled to reopen on June 1 but were delayed because of pending infrastructure and administrative preparations on both sides of the border. tnn(With inputs from Prem Punetha in Pithoragarh)
Article Summary: India and China resume traditional border trade Saturday through Lipulekh in Uttarakhand and Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh. The trade, suspended since 2020 because of Covid, was scheduled to resume on June 1 but was delayed owing to security concerns and inadequate infrastructure.

Article Title: Judge Ujjal Bhuyan questions SC collegium’s opacity
Article Text:
Citizens have right to know deliberations on elevation, transfer of judges: Bhuyan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: SC judge Ujjal Bhuyan has questioned opacity in the collegium’s decisions on judicial appointments.“I have noticed that the last three collegium resolutions contain no reasons whatsoever. Is this a step back from the principle of transparency?” said Justice Bhuyan at a panel discussion on Saturday. “By withholding reasons, we also create space for individuals to enter the judiciary who may later describe groups of people as ‘ants’ and make other remarks that are wholly unconstitutional,” he said.To prevent the entry of such people, “there should be some discussion, there should be some reasons given”, said Justice Ujjal Bhuyan. Though the judge didn’t name anyone, the comment was an apparent reference to a remark by an Allahabad high court judge at a social event in 2024.He was speaking at the launch of the Judicial Transparency Index: Assessing Disclosure of Information by the Supreme Court and the High Courts, prepared by the Justice, Access and Lowering Delays in India (JALDI) Initiative at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy.The judge stressed that deliberations on the elevation and transfer of judges by the SC collegium largely remain confidential, contrary to the principle of judicial transparency.“While carrying out the next assessment on the scale of Judicial Transparency Index, I may request the JALDI team to also look into the aspect of opacity of the collegium system. Deliberations on elevation and transfer of judges remain confidential. Reasons for rejecting or deferring a recommendation are rarely disclosed in full. And the criteria applied are not codified in any publicly disclosed instrument. It is a very important issue. Citizens have a right to know what is happening in the courts. They have a right to know who would be their judges.They have a right to know judgments. These should be in the public domain”, Justice Bhuyan underlined.The report is the first systematic study assessing transparency practices across India’s higher judiciary and evaluates disclosure of information by the Supreme Court and high courts across judicial processes, institutional governance and administration, and judicial and administrative personnel.Referring to a previous collegium resolution reiterating the recommendation of senior advocate Saurabh Kirpal for appointment as a judge, Justice Bhuyan said he found the reasons recorded by the Supreme Court convincing but noted that despite more than three and a half years having passed, no appointment materialised.Key findings of the JALDI report reveal that only five high courts have published a budget on their websites for FY 2025-26 while none has published the criteria governing case allocation.Of the 813 judges in the higher judiciary, only 87 have publicly disclosed their assets even as only two high courts publish disciplinary sanction orders pertaining to district judicial officers.“The findings highlight that the level of judicial transparency varies across courts and demonstrate that while individual disclosure measures have emerged...they have not yet translated into a holistic approach...” a release from Vidhi said.
Article Summary: Justice Ujjal Bhuyan questioned opacity in the collegium’s decisions on judicial appointments. “I have noticed that the last three collegium resolutions contain no reasons whatsoever. Is this a step back from the principle of transparency?” he said.

Article Title: Monsoon hope as WMO sees an El Niño counter
Article Text:

Monsoon may avoid deficient phase with positive IOD

NEW DELHI: The risk of overall monsoon rainfall being ‘below normal’ continues to loom over India due to a strengthening El Niño, but World Meteorological Organisation’s (WMO) latest monthly global seasonal climate update, released late Friday night, offered a ray of hope. It predicted the possibility of a “positive” Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), which could offset to an extent the negative impact of El Niño.El Niño is a climatic pattern of warming of surface waters of central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean and is associated with a weak monsoon and harsher summer in India. IOD, on the other hand, has to do with the difference in sea surface temperatures between western and eastern parts of tropical Indian Ocean. It helps in formation of stronger monsoon winds.“A positive IOD is expected to develop... Combined with exceptionally warm global oceans and the likelihood of a positive IOD, the developing El Niño is expected to shape weather patterns across many parts of the world in the months ahead,” WMO said.If WMO’s forecast comes true, there is a possibility of improved rainfall conditions in south peninsular India — the region which had reported a high cumulative rainfall deficit of 22% as of Aug 1 — in particular and over many parts of the country in general.It may prevent India from slipping from ‘below normal’ phase to ‘deficient’ monsoon phase at the end of the rainy season.El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and IOD are two key factors that govern variation in monsoon rainfall. Though IMD Friday flagged the continuation of “neutral” IOD conditions through the remaining period of southwest (summer) monsoon, it, at the same time, referred to climate forecasts from some international forecasting centres suggesting that positive IOD conditions are likely to develop during Sept.
Article Summary: The risk of overall monsoon rainfall being ‘below normal’ continues to loom over India. World Meteorological Organisation’s (WMO) latest monthly global seasonal climate update, released late Friday night, offered a ray of hope. It predicted the possibility of a “positive” Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), which could offset to an extent the negative impact of El Niño.

NEW DELHI: Review committees of Railway Board have recommended premature retirement of five Group ‘A’ officers in “public interest”, a decision which officials said was aimed at sending out a strong message of “zero tolerance for corruption, lack of integrity and inefficiency”.While two of these officers belong to senior administrative grade (SAG), being equivalent to joint secretary-level officers, the other three are junior administrative grade (JAG) railway officers, who are at director or joint director level. “Integrity, discipline and accountability in public service remain non-negotiable. Actions taken under the provisions of Indian Railway Establishment Code are aimed at upholding these core values,” railway ministry said in an official statement.It said the review committees had carried out detailed assessment of the officers’ service records in accordance with prescribed procedure. The review included examination of annual performance appraisal reports, integrity records, vigilance inputs, disciplinary history and service records. “The committees unanimously recommended premature retirement of the officers in public interest,” the ministry said.The recommendations were made under Indian Railway Establishment Code, which is equivalent to Rule 56(J), dealing with compulsory retirement.In 2022, railways had prematurely retired 32 officers above the age of 50 in “public interest” on grounds of inefficiency, doubtful integrity and conduct unbecoming of a public servant as part of a periodic review. Twenty-two were at the level of director and above.

Article Title: E20: AAP plans pro-choice rally to PM residence

NEW DELHI: Stepping up his campaign against the rollout of E20 fuel, AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal Saturday announced a march to PM’s residence Tuesday to submit petitions against the ethanol-blended fuel programme, while demanding that consumers be given the option to choose betw-een pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations.Addressing AAP’s ‘National Townhall Against E20’ at Constitution Club, Kejriwal alleged Centre had “imposed” ethanol-blended fuel on consumers without adequate consultation and claimed it was causing financial losses to vehicle owners. He said petitions would be collected Monday, before a delegation of about 100 people marches to PM’s residence the following day.Kejriwal placed three demands before Centre -- provide both pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations, price E20 lower than pure petrol, and reduce petrol prices to below Rs 84 per litre. He argued that consumers should be free to decide which fuel they wish to purchase.Claiming govt has repeatedly maintained E20 is safe for vehicles, Kejriwal challenged Centre to make public the scientific studies supporting the policy. “Govt keeps saying studies have found E20 does not damage vehicles. If such studies exist, they should place the reports in the public domain,” he said, adding that several people had shared experiences of reduced mileage and vehicle problems during the town hall.He also alleged govt was only delaying the introduction of higher ethanol blends like E25 and E30 until the controversy surrounding E20 subsides. “There are no studies going on. They are simply waiting for the issue to die down. Once it settles, they will bring E25, E30 and continue increasing the ethanol content,” Kejriwal claimed, advising consumers to opt for electric vehicles until E100-compatible vehicles become commercially available.At the town hall, several owners, mechanics, delivery workers and experts claimed E20 had affected vehicle performance, increased maintenance costs and reduced mileage. Among them was a couple who commute daily from Delhi to Gurgaon. The husband said their 2014 petrol car earlier delivered 14 km per litre but now gives about 9 km per litre, significantly increasing monthly fuel expenses. His wife, who works in the automobile sector, claimed dealerships were receiving complaints from owners of newly-purchased vehicles regarding mileage and performance, but employees had no clear answers to offer.Motorcycle mechanic Aamir Khan, who has been repairing petrol vehicles for over a decade at Bhalswa Dairy, claimed he had witnessed a rise in complaints, particularly from owners of older BS-III and BS-IV vehicles. He advised owners to keep their fuel tanks relatively full to minimise air and moisture accumulation inside the tank.Dr Anupam Saini, an environmental scientist from DU, questioned the environmental benefits of ethanol, saying any assessment should account for fertiliser use, water consumption, land-use change and the overall carbon footprint of ethanol production rather than tailpipe emissions alone.
Article Summary: AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal Saturday announced a march to PM’s residence Tuesday to submit petitions against the ethanol-blended fuel programme. Kejriwal demanded that consumers be given the option to choose betw- een pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations. He said petitions would be collected Monday, before a delegation of about 100 people marches to PM's residence.

Article Title: NEET-PG aspirants to face Aadhaar, iris authentication

NEW DELHI: More than 2.7 lakh medical graduates have registered for NEET-PG 2026, an increase of over 12.5% over last year, as the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences rolls out enhanced authentication measures and candidate-friendly initiatives for the Aug 30 exam.Candidates will undergo Aadhaar-based authentication during registration and on the exam day, while iris-based biometric verification will be used wherever fingerprint authentication is unsuccessful. They will also have to indicate three preferred states for allotment of exam centres, with their correspondence state as mandatory first preference.The test city information will be issued nearly three weeks before the examination, enabling candidates to plan travel and accommodation in advance.The exam will comprise 180 questions that have to be answered in 210 minutes, giving candidates more time per question while retaining the overall exam duration.Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed preparations for the examination Saturday and directed officials to ensure its smooth, transparent and technology-enabled conduct while maintaining the highest standards of security and integrity.He urged candidates not to fall prey to rumours or fraudulent claims regarding question paper leaks, saying the final paper is selected through a highly encrypted, time-bound process shortly before the exam, making any claim of prior access entirely false.Officials said the exam will be conducted under a multi-layered securityframework, which includes CCTV surveillance, biometric authentication, candidate frisking, signal jammers, dynamic computer allocation, live monitoring through central and regional command centres, and independent observers. More than 60,000 exam personnel will be deployed to oversee the process.The end-to-end question paper preparation and delivery process has been reinforced through multiple layers of encryption, secure offline preparation, time-bound finalisation of the paper shortly before the exam and controlled digital decryption at the scheduled commencement of test.NBEMS has also operationalised a dedicated email address to report impersonation, touting and other unfair practices while issuing regular advisories to candidates.
Article Summary: More than 2.7 lakh medical graduates have registered for NEET-PG 2026. This is an increase of over 12.5% over last year. The exam will comprise 180 questions that have to be answered in 210 minutes. More than 60,000 exam personnel will be deployed to oversee the process.

NEW DELHI: Cabinet Friday approved two strategic tunnel projects and the approach roads on NH-244 in J&K at an estimated cost of around Rs 9,800 crore to provide all-weather connectivity between Kashmir Valley and Jammu region while improving access to Chenab Valley,.The projects comprise Singhpora-Vailoo tunnel and Sudhmahadev-Dranga tunnel, along with their approach roads, on the Anantnag-Chenani corridor. These are expected to strengthen road connectivity in Doda, Kishtwar and Udhampur districts, and reduce travel time.While the development of the 39km Singhapora-Vailoo stretch will have 10km unidirectional twin-tube tunnels, the 13km Sudhmahadev-Dranga section will have 8km tunnels. The projects would be completed in five years and will be fully Centre-funded.The tunnels are aimed at bypassing difficult stretches of NH-244 that are frequently affected by adverse weather disrupting traffic and isolating several areas during the winter months. Once completed, the projects will provide a safer and more efficient route for commuters, tourists and freight movement. Officials said the projects would boost regional connectivity by ensuring year-round access to remote districts.

Article Title: July GST collections up 15.4% to Rs 2.1 L cr on higher imports
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: GST collections rose 15.4% to Rs 2,11,205 crore in July, the second highest since the new structure was implemented last Sept, on the back of a 29% jump in integrated GST (IGST) on imports. This was also the highest pace of growth since rate rationalisation.The rise in IGST on imports in July (for transactions in the previous month) may be attributed to higher prices of crude and other commodities in the wake of the West Asia conflict.The impact of strong economic activity in June, when factory output grew at its fastest pace in nearly two years, was also visible on the tax numbers, seen as an advance indicator of economic activity. Some of the price hikes in FMCG and automobile sectors would have also buoyed collections. Central GST mop-up was pegged 12.3% higher at just under Rs 40,000 crore, while state GST grew 8.7% to nearly Rs 48,000 crore."The high GST collections tie in very well with the 7.3% increase in industrial production during June. It reflects continued economic resilience despite the challenges in the external environment...Thesteady growth in GST collections each month indicates that overall domestic consumption is becoming largely insulated from seasonal variations and external headwinds," said MS Mani, partner at Deloitte India.Some experts, however, are worried about the continued rise in imports. "...one cannot ignore the elevated levels of import GST collections, which remain a nagging concern. This points to a persistent gap in domestic manufacturing capability despite the range of successful PLI and Atmanirbhar Bharat interventions rolled out over the past few years.It is likely that the sustained push by policymakers towards localisation of around 100 products (being talked about) over a period of time will help bridge this gap," said Saurabh Agarwal, partner at EY India, a consulting firm.Net of refunds, which were 13% higher at almost Rs 30,000 crore, collections went up 15.8% to Rs 1,81,237 crore.Haryana logged the highest growth of 28%, followed by Gujarat and Puducherry (26%), Karnataka and Goa (23%), and Maharashtra (20%). Chhattisgarh (23% fall), Jharkhand and Manipur (20% decline) were among the laggards.
Article Summary: GST collections rose 15.4% to Rs 2,11,205 crore in July. This was the second highest since the new structure was implemented last Sept. Haryana logged the highest growth of 28%, followed by Gujarat and Puducherry (26%) Karnataka and Goa (23%) and Maharashtra (20%)

Article Title: NEET-PG 2026 gets major overhaul: Centres closer to home, single-shift exam, fewer questions with no change in test duration

NEW DELHI: The Centre has announced a series of changes for the NEET-PG exam to be held later in the month, including expanding the choice of test locations, giving candidates more time to plan travel, and increasing the time available per question.The reforms are aimed at making the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for Postgraduate (NEET-PG) process more convenient and secure, according to the Union health ministry.Under the revised system, candidates will have to provide preferences for three states for their examination centre. Their correspondence state will be the mandatory first preference, allowing allotment of centres closer to their place of residence.Earlier, examination centres were allotted on a first-come, first-served basis, prompting candidates to submit applications immediately after registrations opened. Those who delayed often found nearby centres unavailable and had to travel to other states.Candidates will now be informed of their allotted test city nearly three weeks before the August 30 examination, giving them more time to arrange travel and accommodation.The National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) has also revised the exam pattern, reducing the number of questions from 200 to 180 while keeping the total duration unchanged at 210 minutes. The move will provide candidates with more time per question.The exam was earlier conducted with 200 multiple-choice questions carrying a maximum of 800 marks.The ministry said the question paper preparation and delivery process has been strengthened through multiple layers of encryption, secure offline preparation, time-bound finalisation of papers shortly before the examination, and controlled digital decryption at the start of the test.To further strengthen security, Aadhaar-based authentication has been introduced during registration and on the examination day. Iris-based biometric verification will be used where fingerprint authentication fails.NBEMS has also introduced a dedicated email address for reporting impersonation, touting and other unfair practices, while issuing advisories to candidates to improve awareness and vigilance.NEET-PG 2026 will be conducted in a single shift to ensure uniformity in difficulty level and assessment. In recent years, the exam was conducted in multiple shifts due to emergencies or postponements.Union health minister JP Nadda on Saturday reviewed preparations for the examination and directed agencies to ensure a smooth, secure, transparent and technology-enabled process. He assessed the readiness of NBEMS, technology partners and other stakeholders, and stressed the need for a fair and candidate-friendly examination.A total of 2,73,183 candidates have registered for the medical entrance test, an increase of over 12.5% from last year. The exam will be held in a single shift across around 340 cities and more than 1,300 centres.Security measures include advance sealing and verification of centres, CCTV surveillance, biometric authentication, candidate frisking, deployment of signal jammers, live monitoring through central and regional command centres, and supervision by independent observers and appraisers.More than 60,000 examination functionaries will be deployed for the smooth conduct of the examination, the ministry said.
Article Summary: The reforms are aimed at making the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for Postgraduate (NEET-PG) process more convenient and secure. Candidates will have to provide preferences for three states for their examination centre. The National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) has also revised the exam pattern.

Article Title: Army's intelligence units, Rajasthan police bust counterfeit combat uniform racket in Sriganganagar

NEW DELHI: Busting a big racket on counterfeit military uniforms, a joint operation by Indian Army’s intelligence units and Rajasthan police has led to the seizure of nearly 1,000 metres of unauthorised army-pattern combat cloth from shops across the state’s Sriganganagar district.Acting on a lead, intelligence personnel of the Indian Army carried out a discrete investigation in the city, which pointed to a local firm, as a key link in the supply chain allegedly distributing counterfeit army-pattern combat cloth to shops in Sriganganagar town as well as Lalgarh Jattan, Suratgarh and other nearby markets, the Indian Army said.An interim investigation report was shared with Rajasthan police in mid-July, leading to a coordinated operation on July 30 in which security personnel and police searched multiple shops across the district. The raids yielded approximately 1,000 metres of unauthorised, new-pattern counterfeit combat cloth, exposing a wider network allegedly supplying counterfeit military uniforms to vendors in the region, the Army said.The action followed a seizure of similar counterfeit combat cloth in Bareilly in June this year, which was traced back to a manufacturing source in Sriganganagar.Radical elements and terrorists had in the past exploited open-market military fatigues to infiltrate high-security zones or stage attacks such as in Pathankot and J&K.In India, unauthorised sale, production or storage of official military-pattern camouflage cloth is heavily restricted and banned by local civil administrations in many sensitive regions. Section 168 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 punishes any civilian who unlawfully wears military uniforms or carries tokens of the Indian armed forces with the intent to trick others into believing they are a soldier, sailor or airman.Furthermore, the Indian Army holds exclusive Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) over its digital camouflage pattern design, making commercial reproduction by open-market vendors illegal.
Article Summary: A joint operation by Indian Army’s intelligence units and Rajasthan police has led to the seizure of nearly 1,000 metres of unauthorised army-pattern combat cloth. The action followed a seizure of similar counterfeit combat cloth in Bareilly in June this year.

Article Title: Wife not entitled to interim maintenance if adultery allegation is prima facie true: SC
Article Text:
A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Vipul M Pancholi quashed the order of Rajasthan High Court which had held that a wife cannot be denied interim maintenance during pendency of the husband’s application

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday ruled that a wife cannot be granted interim maintenance if an allegation of adultery is made against her which, at first glance, looks true.A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Vipul M Pancholi quashed the order of the Rajasthan High Court which had held that a wife cannot be denied interim maintenance during pendency of the husband’s application under Section 125(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code relating to adultery. It allowed the plea of a husband who approached the court through lawyer Prabhjit Jauhar against the orders of a trial court and HC rejecting his plea to examine allegations of adultery before granting interim maintenance.“It is obvious that when a case is sought to be proved by circumstantial evidence, it requires a detailed study of the circumstances presented. The evidence furnished in support thereof, including verification, particularly when the evidence in question is electronic, etc. These procedures are bound to take time. Since the stipulation in Section 125 (4) is that if adultery is proved, the wife would neither be entitled to interim nor final maintenance, we are of the view that if a husband files an application under Section 125(4) and is, at the first instance, able to establish the charge through evidence ex facie, then only, there can be said to be a bar to interim maintenance,” the bench said.It added that the trial court and HC clearly fell into error to hold that it was only at the stage of final adjudication that such a question could be decided. “This view would render otiose what has been provided in the statute,” it said.Section 125(4) says that no wife shall be entitled to receive an allowance for maintenance or interim maintenance and expenses of proceedings, as the case may be, from her husband if she is living in adultery, or if, without any sufficient reason, she refuses to live with her husband, or if they are living separately by mutual consent.“If the application for maintenance is to be denied at the interim stage itself, the party having filed the application under Section 125(4) must present clear and cogent evidence that would ex-facie establish adultery on the part of the claimant for maintenance,” the bench said.Noting that the husband in the case has placed a large number of photographs and 92 videos to substantiate his allegation against the wife, the court said they were perhaps procured from a private detective and expressed the need to frame a law to regulate the sector as there was an increasing reliance on private investigators to gather information.“We believe that regulation and accountability are equally important in the sphere of private investigation,” it said
Article Summary: A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Vipul M Pancholi quashed the order of the Rajasthan High Court. It allowed the plea of a husband who approached the court through lawyer Prabhjit Jauhar against the orders of a trial court and HC.

Article Title: West Bengal to clear all pending CAA applications within six months, says Suvendu Adhikari
Article Text:
File photo: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari

Nearly 24,000 citizenship certificates issued so far

'CAA was never meant to target anyone'

TMC accused of spreading confusion over CAA

Government to assist beneficiaries

Census exercise and refugee distinction

NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday announced that all pending applications for citizenship under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) in the state would be disposed of within the next six months, asserting that the law was enacted to grant citizenship and not to take it away.Speaking at a CAA citizenship certificate distribution programme in New Town, where around 300 members of the Matua community from North 24 Parganas district received citizenship certificates, Adhikari alleged that the previous Trinamool Congress (TMC) government had spread misinformation about the law for "political gains"."The CAA is meant to grant citizenship, not to take away anyone's citizenship," Adhikari said, as quoted by news agency PTI.He urged all eligible applicants to come forward and apply under the Act, saying more citizenship certificates would be issued in the coming months.Presenting the state's progress in implementing the CAA, Adhikari said 23,956 citizenship certificates had been issued so far, including 5,966 certificates over the past 11 weeks since the BJP government assumed office.According to him, the state has received 2,30,605 applications under the CAA.He said Nadia district has recorded the highest number of beneficiaries with 10,191 citizenship certificates, followed by North 24 Parganas with 8,930 certificates.Adhikari also said that, following discussions with the Union home secretary, the process of delegating legal and administrative powers to district magistrates for the speedy disposal of CAA applications is expected to begin within a month."Following discussions with the Union home secretary, the process of delegating legal and administrative powers to district magistrates for the speedy disposal of CAA applications is expected to begin within a month," he said.He noted that district magistrates in Gujarat and Rajasthan already exercise such powers.The chief minister reiterated that the Citizenship (Amendment) Act was introduced to grant Indian citizenship to eligible refugees and not to deprive anyone of their rights.The CAA, passed by Parliament in 2019, provides a pathway to Indian citizenship for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians who fled religious persecution in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan and entered India on or before December 31, 2014.Recalling the BJP's promise on citizenship, Adhikari said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had assured members of the Matua community before the 2019 Lok Sabha elections that eligible refugees from Bangladesh would receive Indian citizenship.He said the rules under the Act were eventually notified on March 6, 2024, after implementation was delayed due to the Covid-19 pandemic.Targeting the previous TMC government, Adhikari alleged that it deliberately equated the CAA with the National Register of Citizens (NRC), creating confusion among people, particularly Muslims."The previous government projected the CAA as the NRC and misled the people, particularly the Muslim community. False propaganda was spread claiming that applying under the CAA would result in the loss of jobs, ration benefits or the Lakshmir Bhandar financial assistance scheme," he alleged.He claimed that government property had been vandalised during protests triggered by such misinformation and said, "Today, the truth has come out, and even MLAs from the opposition have attended this government programme voluntarily."Adhikari said the state government would take steps to help eligible CAA beneficiaries who continue to face legal proceedings or remain in jail because of documentation-related issues by facilitating their release on bail.He added that the state police had been instructed to ensure that no eligible applicant faced harassment in matters related to the CAA.The state government will also facilitate the inclusion of beneficiaries' names in electoral rolls after citizenship is granted and ensure that eligible applicants receive Scheduled Caste certificates in a time-bound manner.One of the beneficiaries, a woman refugee originally from Bagerhat in Bangladesh, thanked the government after receiving her citizenship certificate."I lived in Bagerhat in Bangladesh and came to India in 2006. I had been living in fear for so many years. I thank the Prime Minister and the chief minister," she said, as cited by PTI.The announcement comes as West Bengal began the self-enumeration phase of the country's 16th Census.Adhikari had said the Census exercise and illegal immigration were separate issues, while distinguishing between illegal immigrants and refugees covered under the CAA.He had maintained that refugees eligible under the CAA would be protected, while illegal immigrants would not be entitled to government welfare benefits.He also said the Census would help create a permanent database for delivering government welfare schemes more efficiently.
Article Summary: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari says all pending applications for citizenship under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) in the state will be disposed of within the next six months. The CAA, passed by Parliament in 2019, provides a pathway to Indian citizenship for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians.

Come to Bengal as many times as you want. It is my duty as CM to provide you with security whenever you visit Bengal," Adhikari said.The remarks came a day after Nasreen made her first public visit to Kolkata in nearly two decades, describing her return as an emotional homecoming.Nasreen returned to Kolkata on Friday, marking her first public appearance in the city since 2007, when widespread protests over her memoir "Dwikhandito" forced her to leave the state.Speaking on her return, the exiled writer said coming back to Kolkata felt like returning to "my own country."Nasreen had taken refuge in India after fleeing Bangladesh in the 1990s following threats over her writings. She lived in Kolkata for several years before leaving the city in 2007 amid protests against Dwikhandito.Her memoir, Dwikhandito ("Split in Two"), was banned by the then Left Front government in West Bengal in 2003 on the grounds that it allegedly hurt the religious sentiments of a section of the Muslim community.The ban and the protests surrounding the book eventually led to Nasreen leaving Kolkata, where she had been living in exile.Her latest visit has reignited discussions on freedom of expression, the treatment of exiled writers and West Bengal's political climate, with Adhikari using the occasion to assure her of protection during future visits to the state.
Article Summary: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari assured exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasreen of full security during her visits to the state. Nasreen returned to Kolkata on Friday, marking her first public appearance in the city since 2007. Her memoir, Dwikhandito, was banned by the then Left Front government in West Bengal in 2003.

Article Title: More tests, less health: Why India might be testing itself sick
Article Text:
India's quiet overtesting crisis (AI-generated image)

When does a test actually become necessary?



India's overtesting epidemic (AI generated image)

Regulation that hasn't caught up

The anxiety economy



The anxiety economy (AI generated image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Walk into any diagnostics lab in a major Indian city and you will likely be handed a laminated menu, not of food, but of the body. Silver package, gold package, platinum package. Forty tests, sixty tests, ninety. Fasting blood sugar, thyroid panels, vitamin D, cardiac markers, tumour markers, all bundled together and priced to feel like a bargain rather than a medical decision. Nobody asks whether these tests were prescribed by a doctor, because increasingly, they aren't. They are sold.This is the quieter side of India's healthcare story, one that gets far less attention than the shortage of hospital beds or the scarcity of rural doctors. In the country's cities, among its insured and upwardly mobile, a different problem has taken root: too much testing, too often, for too little reason. Corporate wellness programmes hand out annual full-body checkups as a perk. Insurance companies fold preventive panels into premium plans as a selling point.Diagnostic chains run festive discounts on scans the way electronics stores discount televisions. The result is a population of healthy, asymptomatic people walking out with reports listing dozens of parameters, several flagged in borderline yellow, and no doctor in the room to explain what any of it means.The consequences are not trivial. Overtesting drives a cascade, a mildly abnormal number on an unnecessary test leads to a follow-up scan, which leads to a biopsy, which leads to weeks of anxiety over something that may never have caused harm.Doctors describe patients arriving with thick folders of test results and no clinical complaint, unsure why they were tested in the first place, but certain that more tests must mean better health.The question this raises is not whether early detection saves lives, it does, but whether India's growing test-industrial complex has confused detection with reassurance, and reassurance with health.Ask a doctor practising evidence-based medicine when a test is warranted, and the answer rarely begins with the test itself. It begins with a conversation."It's an individualised question," says Dr. Haripriya Jagadish, Internal Medicine Specialist at Apollo Spectra Hospital, Chennai. "Most practitioners go by evidence-based medicine. The doctor will elicit the history, which will include all the symptoms of the patient, and based on that, the tests are done."That process, history-taking, is the part of clinical practice most invisible to the patient and most absent from the retail model of testing. A doctor working through a patient's symptoms, duration, family history and risk factors is, in effect, narrowing a list of possibilities before ordering a single test, so that each test serves to confirm or rule out something specific. A preventive package sold off a billboard skips that step entirely, running dozens of tests without first asking what, if anything, the patient's body is signalling.According to Dr Jagadish, the reasons a test is actually indicated tend to fall into a few well-defined categories. "The common reasons start from infections, chronic diseases, inflammation and malignancy," she says. "Everything is based on the symptoms and the science." An unexplained fever might point toward an infection workup. Unexplained fatigue or weight change, paired with family history, might justify screening for a chronic condition such as diabetes or thyroid dysfunction. Persistent, localised pain or an abnormal finding on physical examination might warrant investigation for inflammation or, in some cases, malignancy. In each instance, the test follows the symptom, not the other way around.This is the clinical logic that preventive test packages tend to bypass. Rather than starting with a patient's history and narrowing toward a hypothesis, they start with a menu of everything available and work backward, hoping that volume compensates for the absence of a clinical question. For Dr. Jagadish 's generation of evidence-based practitioners, that inversion is precisely the problem, not that testing itself is harmful, but that testing without a preceding clinical reason strips it of the context needed to interpret what the results actually mean.When a pharmaceutical company in India wants to advertise a prescription drug to the public, the law steps in, such advertising is restricted, and in most cases requires government authorisation before it can run. When a diagnostics chain wants to advertise a bundle of forty preventive tests, including several with genuine cancer-screening implications, no equivalent threshold exists. The test package occupies a regulatory blind spot: not quite a drug, not quite a medical procedure requiring a prescription, and therefore largely free to be marketed the way any consumer product would be, with discounts, urgency, and appeals to fear.India's oversight of diagnostic laboratories does exist, but it is aimed almost entirely at technical quality, accreditation bodies set standards for how accurately a lab must run a test, not for whether that test should have been sold to an asymptomatic customer in the first place, or how the results should be communicated once they arrive. There is no requirement that a preventive test package be accompanied by pre-test counselling, no mandate that a qualified clinician interpret results before they reach the patient, and no restriction on marketing screening tests directly to consumers with no clinical indication.This is not a uniquely Indian problem, direct-to-consumer testing has expanded globally, and regulators in some markets have begun responding, tightening requirements around what claims these tests can make and how aggressively they can be marketed to healthy people. What distinguishes India is the pace of that catch-up. As the market for retail diagnostics has scaled rapidly across metros and now smaller cities, the regulatory apparatus governing how these tests are sold, and to whom, has largely stayed where it was decades ago, built for an era when a blood test still required a doctor to ask for it.The report itself rarely arrives with context. It arrives as a PDF or a printed sheet, rows of values, reference ranges in brackets, and a handful highlighted in red or yellow, with no accompanying explanation of what those deviations actually mean for a specific person's health. For a patient with no symptoms and no clinical history prompting the test, that ambiguity becomes fertile ground for anxiety.The pattern is a familiar one to clinicians. A mildly elevated tumour marker, a borderline nodule on an incidental scan, a number just outside the "normal" range on a test that was never clinically indicated in the first place, these findings, once flagged, tend to set off a cascade. The patient seeks a specialist opinion. The specialist, unable to rule out concern from a single data point, orders a follow-up scan or a repeat test. In some cases, that escalates further to a biopsy or invasive procedure, undertaken to investigate a finding that may have had no clinical significance to begin with.Dr Jagadish points to this as one of the central risks of indiscriminate testing. "The problem with getting too many tests, especially ones like cancer screening, is when you do them and get an abnormal value, unless there's a medical correlation, it can do more harm than good," she says. "Especially this generation has a lot of anxiety around that. It unnecessarily drives up the medical cost of the patient as well as the psychological trauma. "That psychological toll rarely features in conversations about overtesting, which tend to focus on financial waste or clinical inefficiency. But for the patient sitting with an unexplained abnormal result, the experience is rarely just administrative. It is weeks of uncertainty, repeated consultations, and a growing preoccupation with a number that may resolve on its own, or may never have meant anything at all. For a generation already primed toward health anxiety, amplified by symptom-checking apps, wellness content and a culture that treats more data as inherently reassuring, an unexplained flagged result can be harder to sit with than the absence of information ever was.What gets lost in this cycle is the fact that not every abnormality requires action. Medicine has long understood that some findings are incidental, present, but clinically irrelevant, yet a system that tests first and interprets later leaves little room for that nuance. The result is a quiet, largely undocumented cost of overtesting: not just money spent on unnecessary follow-ups, but the accumulated weight of worry carried by people who were never actually sick.
Article Summary: India's growing test-industrial complex has confused detection with reassurance. Corporate wellness programmes hand out annual full-body checkups as a perk. Insurance companies fold preventive panels into premium plans. Diagnostic chains run festive discounts on scans the way electronics stores discount televisions.

According to FSSAI, the unit failed to comply with several regulatory and hygiene requirements, including inadequate quality management systems and deficiencies in manufacturing practices.FSSAI also issued a prohibition order against M/s Vatave Health Care, banning the manufacture, storage, distribution and sale of its Folineuro Syrup (Folinic Acid Syrup). The regulator said the product was marketed as a nutritional food supplement with misleading claims related to brain function despite not complying with provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act and the Food Safety and Standards (Health Supplements, Nutraceuticals, Food for Special Dietary Use, Food for Special Medical Purpose, Functional Food and Novel Food) Regulations, 2016.The regulator said the actions were taken to protect consumers and ensure compliance with food safety laws. It warned that violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, would invite strict legal and penal action.
Article Summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has launched a fresh enforcement drive against food business operators. The regulator has issued a product recall, suspended a manufacturing licence and prohibited the sale of a health supplement over serious violations of food safety regulations.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday granted interim protection from arrest to DMK leader and former Tamil Nadu minister V Senthil Balaji in the alleged TASMAC corruption case. The court directed Balaji to deposit his passport, cooperate with the investigation and refrain from influencing witnesses while granting him relief.A Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi stayed the operation of FIR No. 05 of 2026 and issued notice to the Tamil Nadu government on Balaji's plea challenging the Madras high court's refusal to grant anticipatory bail."Subject to the petitioner fully cooperating with the probe, his arrest shall remain stayed. He is directed to deposit his passport with the Investigating Officer. FIR No. 05 of 2026 dated July 8 shall remain stayed. He shall not attempt to influence witnesses," the Bench directed, ANI reported.The FIR was registered by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) following the Madras high court's refusal to grant anticipatory bail to Balaji in the alleged TASMAC scam involving purported irregularities in the allotment of liquor shops and bars.During the hearing, the Supreme Court questioned whether the police should have conducted a preliminary enquiry before registering the FIR, observing that it appeared to be based largely on an affidavit filed by the Enforcement Directorate (ED).The Bench also noted that the allegations primarily related to the period between 2020 and 2021 and observed that Balaji was no longer a minister."He is no longer a Minister," the Court remarked, adding that "if an independent investigation found him guilty, he is bound to face consequences."Senior advocate Amit Anand Tiwari, appearing for Balaji along with senior advocates Kapil Sibal and Mukul Rohatgi, argued that custodial interrogation was unnecessary."Our contention is that the FIR is for the incident said to have taken place between 2021 and 2025. I am at no flight risk; no custodial interrogation required. I was the minister in the department and TASMAC is a corporation independent in existence and functioning," Tiwari submitted, according to PTI.Balaji also contended that the FIR substantially reproduced the Enforcement Directorate's affidavit and petition filed before the Supreme Court."In fact, the FIR itself at various places says that it is from the counter affidavit and petition of the ED," his plea stated.Opposing the plea, the Tamil Nadu government argued that Balaji continued to wield considerable influence despite no longer holding office."From 2021 to 2025, he was in power and did not let any complaint sustain against him. We will have a problem if the evidence goes away. Considering the kind of scam that has happened and his antecedents--there are at least six serious cases," the prosecution submitted.The State further argued, "Even if he is not in power, he is able to carry on the influence."Justice Bagchi, however, said the State's concerns could be addressed by imposing appropriate safeguards."He is not going to abscond, as you say. We will ensure that he does not abscond, participates in the investigation and does not interfere with the probe. If there is any breach, we will interfere," Justice Bagchi observed.Chief Justice of India Surya Kant also stressed that the investigation should proceed independently."Hold an independent probe. If he is guilty, he will face..." the Chief Justice observed.While granting interim protection, Justice Bagchi cautioned Balaji's counsel that any violation of the conditions would invite immediate action.The Supreme Court's order came a day after senior advocates Kapil Sibal and Mukul Rohatgi sought an urgent hearing, arguing that Balaji faced imminent coercive action following the Madras high court's refusal to grant anticipatory bail.The case stems from allegations of a large-scale cash kickback scheme in TASMAC involving the allotment of liquor shops and bars.
