The court directed Balaji to deposit his passport, cooperate with the investigation and refrain from influencing witnesses. The case stems from allegations of a large-scale cash kickback in the allotment of liquor shops and bars.

Article Title: ‘Normal’ July rain defies forecast of El Nino impact
Article Text:
Monsoon in India (representative image)

El Niño alone can no more explain India’s rain pattern: Experts

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s monsoon has delivered a surprise this July, defying forecasts of below-normal rainfall despite a strengthening El Nino and reinforcing scientists’ warnings that climate change is altering the country’s most important weather system, report Chittaranjan Tembhekar & Gaurav Talwar.As of July 30, India received 270.1mm of rains in July against a normal of 271.9mm, well within normal range. IMD had said July rainfall was likely to be less than 94% of long period average.However, rainfall distribution remained skewed, with central India receiving 29% excess in July while the east & northeast recorded a deficit of 30% and south 28%.The monsoon deficit since June 1 was 14%. The unexpected turnaround in July has eased fears of a big monsoon shortfall but highlighted a new reality: long dry spells interspersed with short bursts of extremely heavy rain capable of triggering floods and landslides.According to a Climate Trends briefing, successive weather systems cut the national rainfall deficit considerably from 40% at the end of June.Scientists say the biggest lesson from monsoon 2026 is that El Niño alone can no longer explain India’s rainfall behaviour.Global warming, warming oceans and changing atmospheric circulation are increasingly interacting with traditional climate drivers, making monsoon forecasts more difficult.“The challenge is no longer predicting how much rain India will receive, but forecasting where, when and how intensely it will fall in a warming climate,” scientists said.Rainfall remained highly uneven. While 16 meteorological subdivisions states recorded normal rainfall in the season and three saw excess to large-excess rainfall, 17 subdivisions remained deficient. Central India was almost normal with a 1% surplus, northwest India had an 11% shortfall, while east and northeast India remained 30% below normal and south India 25% deficient.The findings are particularly striking because the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has projected an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño developing between Oct and Dec — a pattern usually associated with weaker Indian monsoons.Former IMD director general K J Ramesh attributed July’s recovery to abnormal warming over the western Pacific, which spawned successive monsoon systems over the Bay of Bengal, and the increasing influence of Western Disturbances that enhanced rainfall over Maharashtra and Gujarat.“Climate change is reshaping the characteristics of the monsoon, which existing models are failing to take into account,” Ramesh said.Akshay Deoras of the University of Reading said the monsoon rebounded rapidly after an early July lull. He cited Umbergaon in Gujarat receiving 1,064 mm of rain in 24 hours —among the highest daily totals recorded since 1901 — as evidence of intensifying rainfall extremes, adding that climate change appears to be amplifying the monsoon’s internal weather systems.
Article Summary: India received 270.1mm of rains in July against a normal of 271.9mm, well within normal range. But rainfall distribution remained skewed, with central India receiving 29% excess in July while the east & northeast recorded a deficit of 30% and south 28%.

Article Title: RTI activist seeks inquiry into Abhijeet Dipke's father's finances; flags Rs 1 crore CJP defence fund
Article Text:
(With agency inputs)





SURAT: A Surat-based RTI activist on Saturday said he had sought an inquiry into the finances of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke’s father, a retired government employee who had funded his son’s education abroad.Activist Amit Tiwari also said he had written to the Election Commission of India and the Central GST authorities regarding the legal defence fund announced by senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal for CJP protesters facing police cases.Tiwari said he has sought a probe into the financial status of Dipke's father, Bhagwanrao Dipke, a retired Maharashtra government employee, questioning how he was able to fund his son's higher education abroad."The Cockroach Janta Party is an unregistered entity but is operating as a political party....If Rs 1 crore has been pledged to it as a legal defence fund, then the EC should verify whether the CJP is registered with it under section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951," he told PTI."If not registered, then its operation under the name of a political party and collection/receipt of funds may require examination," he said.Tiwari wrote to the CBEC, asking it to examine whether 18% GST would be applicable on the Rs 1 crore pledged by Sibal for the legal defence fund of CJP protesters.On Monday, Sibal announced a contribution of Rs 1 crore to a fund set up by CJP to provide legal aid to protesters arrested by the Delhi Police in connection with the agitation over the NEET paper leak controversy.

Article Title: 'Same people who litter here, use dustbin abroad': Bombay HC on civic sense
Article Text:
The court stressed that maintaining cleanliness is a fundamental duty and called for strict action against offenders. (Generative image)

NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court on Friday came down heavily on Indians who litter public places at home but follow cleanliness rules abroad, saying the same people who "throw garbage on the road without batting an eyelid" in India ensure to put "even a small chocolate wrapper" in the dustbin abroad.The court stressed that maintaining cleanliness is a fundamental duty and called for strict action against offenders.A bench of Justices G S Kulkarni and Aarti Sathe made the observations while hearing a batch of petitions over pollution, foul odour, gas emissions and health hazards linked to the Kanjurmarg dumping ground in Mumbai.The judges said public participation was essential to keeping the city clean and urged civic authorities to enforce the rules without hesitation."If a person wants a clean environment, then he or she has a corresponding fundamental duty towards society to maintain cleanliness. We want the civic officials to be ruthless in taking action," the court said according to news agency PTI.Expressing concern over people's attitude towards public cleanliness, the bench said citizens often behave differently once they leave India."We have to sensitise our citizens. Here, a person will throw garbage on the road without batting an eyelid, but these same people, when abroad, will strictly avoid such behaviour.Even a small chocolate wrapper they will throw in the dustbin," the high court said.The bench then questioned, "Is this the price of liberty and democracy?"The court also voiced concern over the large quantity of plastic waste strewn across public places, observing that even Mumbai's beaches are littered with plastic. It questioned whether such conditions reflected the standards of "a civilised society".The judges noted that garbage dumped on roads and in narrow lanes poses serious health and hygiene risks to residents every day.Referring to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai's slogan 'Swachch Mumbai, Sundar Mumbai, Aapli Mumbai, Sundar Mumbai', the court said the civic body's intention was commendable but was being undermined by irresponsible behaviour from citizens and inadequate enforcement by the municipal machinery."It is in these circumstances the role of MCGM's cleanliness machinery wardwise becomes significant, to take all effective steps so that public streets are not used by the citizens as dumping places," the bench observed.The court said failing to enforce the rules would defeat the objective behind the civic body's cleanliness campaign and urged authorities to implement the existing regulations strictly.It also raised concerns over the handling of garbage near heritage landmarks such as Rajabai Tower and the Bombay high court building. The bench observed that tourists, including foreign visitors, often encounter garbage on roads because of poor waste handling by municipal collection vehicles.The high court directed the civic body to take corrective steps within a week, warning that it would otherwise be compelled to pass further orders.
Article Summary: The court stressed that maintaining cleanliness is a fundamental duty and called for strict action against offenders. Justices G S Kulkarni and Aarti Sathe made the observations while hearing a batch of petitions over pollution, foul odour, gas emissions and health hazards linked to the Kanjurmarg dumping ground.

Article Title: Petrol would've hit Rs 125/litre in Delhi without ethanol blend, says govt
Article Text:
The petroleum ministry defended ethanol blending, stating it saved consumers nearly thirty rupees per litre.





NEW DELHI: Petrol in Delhi would have cost around Rs 125 a litre when global crude prices touched $135 a barrel, had oil companies not blended ethanol into the fuel, the petroleum ministry said on Friday, defending the ethanol programme against claims about its costs, food security impact, and alleged taxpayer subsidy.The ministry said consumers instead paid Rs 94.77 per litre, since ethanol — procured domestically at pre-agreed prices — made up 20% of every litre and helped insulate retail prices from the crude spike, saving nearly Rs 30 a litre at the peak of the crisis.The government held petrol and diesel prices steady for nearly 75 days after the West Asia conflict began on February 28, before raising them by Rs 7.5 a litre in May. Standard E20 petrol (91-octane) now costs Rs 102.12 a litre in Delhi, while 100-octane petrol is priced at Rs 169.The ministry also denied allegations that foodgrain meant for the poor was being diverted for ethanol production, or that subsidised FCI rice was being used to support the programme.On the question of fuel efficiency, the road transport ministry — citing a study by ARAI, SIAM and IOC — told the Lok Sabha on Thursday that BS-III, BS-IV and BS-VI vehicles designed for E10 fuel may see efficiency drop by 2-6% depending on vehicle category and age when run on E20.The oil ministry had earlier told the Rajya Sabha on July 20 that the reduction in such vehicles is limited to about 3-5%.Both ministries said the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme was rolled out through a phased, scientifically validated process, with blending levels raised gradually as production capacity and infrastructure were built up. Road transport minister Nitin Gadkari told the Lok Sabha that the shift to E20 followed validation of fuel systems, engine durability, drivability, material compatibility and emissions performance, with automakers, oil marketing companies, and the sugar and grain industries consulted throughout.The government added that lab studies and real-world data have shown no adverse impact on vehicle performance from E20 fuel, noting that over 20 crore two-wheelers and 3 crore-plus petrol cars have run on these blends without verified evidence of engine failure linked to ethanol blending.
Article Summary: Petrol in Delhi would have cost around Rs 125 a litre when global crude prices touched $135 a barrel, had oil companies not blended ethanol into the fuel. The petroleum ministry said consumers instead paid Rs 94.77 per litre, since ethanol made up 20% of every litre and helped insulate retail prices from the crude spike. The government held petrol and diesel prices steady for nearly 75 days after the West Asia conflict began.

Article Title: US makes $20,000 visa bond programme permanent; India not on 50-country list
Article Text:
India not on list

Who will be affected?

The US State Department has decided to make its visa bond programme permanent after successfully running it as a pilot scheme, expanding a policy aimed at reducing visa overstays. The programme currently applies to citizens of 50 countries.Under the new rule, consular officers may require certain applicants for US visitor visas to post a bond of up to $20,000 before a visa is issued. The regulation takes effect on August 3, when it is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register. US officials have indicated that additional countries could be added to the programme in the future, Reuters cites.The visa bond programme currently covers citizens of 50 countries, including Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan, but India is not among them. This means Indian applicants for B-1 (business) and B-2 (tourist) visas are not affected by the new rule at present.However, the State Department has indicated that more countries could be added to the programme in the future.The rule applies to applicants seeking B-1 (business) and B-2 (tourism) visas from countries covered under the programme.According to the Federal Register notice, "Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers."The State Department said a year-long review of the pilot programme found that visa bonds were effective in encouraging travellers to comply with the terms of their stay in the United States.During the pilot programme launched in 2025, consular officers could require visa applicants to post bonds of $5,000, $10,000 or $15,000.Under the permanent rule, the $5,000 option has been removed and the maximum bond amount has been increased to $20,000.Immigration and rights advocates have criticised the policy, arguing that requiring applicants to deposit thousands of dollars could discourage legitimate travel to the United States.The visa bond programme is part of a broader immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump.
Article Summary: The US State Department has decided to make its visa bond programme permanent. The programme is aimed at reducing visa overstays. It currently covers citizens of 50 countries, including Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan. India is not among them. The regulation takes effect on August 3, when it is published in the Federal Register.

Article Title: China spent decades moving water across a continent. The world's largest diversion project now serves 185 million people
Article Text:
Representative Image of China's South-to-North Water Diversion Project (AI-generated image)

Why China decided to move water across the country

How much water the project actually moves

Why the project required relocating hundreds of thousands of people

What environmental concerns the project has raised

What the project's completion is expected to look like

In 2002, China's State Council formally approved construction of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, an engineering undertaking designed to move water from the relatively water-rich Yangtze River basin in the south to the chronically dry cities and farmland of northern China, including Beijing. More than two decades later, the project stands as the largest water transfer scheme ever built anywhere in the world, moving tens of billions of cubic metres of water annually through thousands of kilometres of canals, tunnels and aqueducts. According to Chinese authorities, more than 185 million people across northern China have directly benefited from the water it now delivers. Achieving that scale came at a high human cost, with at least 330,000 residents relocated from their homes to make way for the project's reservoirs and canals.Northern China, including the capital Beijing, is home to roughly half the country's population but only a small share of its water resources, a structural imbalance that has driven chronic water scarcity across the region for decades. According to a comprehensive review published in the peer-reviewed journal Water , the idea of transferring water from the south to the north was first proposed by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1952, though the government lacked the financial resources and engineering capability to act on it for decades.It was only after extensive feasibility studies through the 1990s that the State Council formally approved the project's master plan in 2002, with construction beginning that same year.The project was designed around three separate routes, the Eastern, Central and a still incomplete Western route, each drawing water from a different point along the Yangtze River basin and channelling it north through a combination of new canals and, in the case of the Eastern route, sections of the centuries-old Grand Canal.According to an official statement from the Chinese government , released by China's Ministry of Water Resources in December 2024, the project's middle and eastern routes had by that point diverted more than 76.7 billion cubic metres of water to northern China over the preceding decade, directly benefiting over 185 million people. The ministry credited the project with supporting more than 16 trillion yuan, or roughly 2.23 trillion US dollars, in GDP growth across northern China's water-dependent regions.The Central Route, sometimes referred to as the Grand Aqueduct, draws water from the Danjiangkou Reservoir on a tributary of the Yangtze and channels it more than 1,200 kilometres north, largely using gravity rather than mechanical pumping, reaching Beijing after its completion in 2014. The Eastern Route, built partly along the historic path of the Grand Canal, moves water toward Tianjin and other cities in the country's northeast.Raising the water level of the Danjiangkou Reservoir to supply the Central Route required flooding land across parts of Hubei and Henan provinces, forcing the relocation of communities that had lived along the reservoir's edges for generations. Roughly 330,000 people were relocated as part of this process, described at the time as one of the largest engineering-driven resettlements in China's modern history.According to the Water journal review, this resettlement effort brought significant disruption to displaced communities, many of whom had to abandon established livelihoods such as fruit farming and fishing for new occupations in unfamiliar locations. Reports from residents in subsequent years pointed to ongoing frustrations, including disputes over compensation, housing quality and lost income, with some displaced families formally petitioning local authorities over these grievances well after their initial relocation.Beyond the human cost of relocation, researchers have also flagged a range of environmental consequences tied to the project's scale. According to the Water journal review, these include altered river ecology along the Yangtze and Han river systems, concerns over water quality and pollutant transfer between river basins that were never naturally connected, and risks to biodiversity in areas affected by reduced downstream flow, particularly along the Han River, which feeds the Central Route's main reservoir.The review also notes that the project's total projected cost, once fully completed, is expected to run into the tens of billions of dollars, making it not only the largest water transfer scheme in the world by volume, but also among the most expensive single infrastructure projects China has ever undertaken.China's Ministry of Water Resources has stated that the full three-route system is intended to transfer roughly 44.8 cubic kilometres of water annually once completed, with a target completion date set for 2050. The still unfinished Western route, intended to draw water from the upper reaches of the Yangtze basin across difficult, high-altitude terrain, remains the most technically and environmentally challenging phase of the project and continues to be studied rather than actively constructed.More than two decades after ground was first broken, the South-to-North Water Diversion Project stands as a striking example of the scale modern infrastructure can reach when a government commits to fundamentally reshaping a country's water geography, delivering measurable benefits to hundreds of millions of people in the water stressed north, while leaving a lasting and still unresolved legacy for the hundreds of thousands of residents who were displaced to make it possible.
Article Summary: China's South-to-North Water Diversion Project is the largest water transfer scheme ever built anywhere in the world. It aims to move water from the relatively water-rich Yangtze River basin in the south to the chronically dry cities and farmland of northern China. Achieving that scale came at a high human cost, with at least 330,000 residents relocated from their homes to make way for the project's reservoirs.

Article Title: In the 1950s, California oceanographer John D. Isaacs proposed towing an 8-billion-tonne Antarctic iceberg to San Diego, but the frozen reservoir never arrived
Article Text:
Tabular Iceberg in Antarctic waters. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A radical solution to California’s growing water requirement

Icebergs of Lemaire in Antarctic waters. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why the proposal never made further progress

Long before desalination plants became common and climate change intensified concerns regarding water security, one California oceanographer proposed an idea that sounded more like science fiction than engineering. In the mid-1950s, Dr John D. Isaacs of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography suggested towing a colossal Antarctic iceberg across the Pacific Ocean to Southern California. Notably, his original proposal, formulated in his 1949 classes and expanded in the February 1956 issue of Science Digest, specifically suggested utilizing the Humboldt Current to deliver the Antarctic iceberg to the coast of Southern California to supply water to Los Angeles. According to NOAA’s historical bibliography , Icebergs for Use as Freshwater, Isaacs envisioned using a fleet of powerful tugboats to haul a tabular iceberg that weighed about 8 billion tonnes to San Diego, where the berg’s freshwater could help meet the requirements of a growing population. While the project never progressed beyond the conceptual stage, it sparked decades of scientific and engineering research into whether icebergs could one day be used as freshwater reservoirs during drought-heavy situations.According to NOAA bibliography and historical reviews published in the Annals of Glaciology , Isaacs believed Antarctica contained an immense reserve of freshwater locked inside naturally calved tabular icebergs.Rather than mining glaciers or constructing vast reservoirs, he proposed to capture one of these floating ice masses and to tow it northward using several oceangoing tugboats. As the NOAA report notes, earlier estimates suggested the voyage could take several months, and materials or protective covering might reduce melting during transport. It is worth noting that while Isaacs never formally published an engineering paper on the proposal, his calculations were widely discussed in scientific circles and popular science publications during the 1950s, thus inspiring researchers to analyse whether transporting freshwater in the form of an iceberg could be technically feasible.The concept drew more attention during the 1970s as freshwater shortages became a growing global concern. According to the NOAA bibliography, researchers at the RAND Corporation produced detailed feasibility reports on transporting ice masses from Antarctica. Notably, the first International Conference on Iceberg Utilisation convened in Iowa in 1977, bringing together glaciologists, engineers and policymakers from around the world. The conference examined towing strategies, melting rates, engineering challenges and economic feasibility, marking the first coordinated international effort to evaluate iceberg harvesting as a potential water-crisis solution.According to the Annals of Glaciology, scientists quickly identified major barriers to the proposal, including melting, wave erosion, towing forces, iceberg stability and operational costs. They explained that a single Antarctic iceberg large enough to justify transport would require several high-powered tugboats operating continuously for months while navigating unpredictable ocean conditions and storms. Furthermore, the researchers of the Annals of Glaciology recognised that waves erode bergs' edges much faster than simple atmospheric melting, meaning a significant proportion of the freshwater could disappear before reaching its destination.Despite this, Isaacs’ idea fundamentally changed scientific thinking, as according to NOAA’s bibliography, the concept inspired decades of research into iceberg towing, drag measurements, insulation systems and freshwater economics. Notably, later studies investigated ice mass transport not only to Southern California but also to Saudi Arabia, Australia and other water-stressed regions. Advances in numerical modelling, satellite observations and polar engineering have since provided far more sophisticated tools for evaluating the concept than were available in the past.While no Antarctic iceberg has ever been towed to California, Isaacs’ ambitious vision continues to influence modern research. Recent iceberg towing studies suggest that advances in marine engineering and climate science have transformed what was once dismissed as an eccentric proposal into a subject of serious study. Meanwhile, desalination, recycling and conservation efforts remain the dominant solutions for water scarcity; the notion of using Earth’s largest floating freshwater reservoirs has never completely disappeared.
Article Summary: In the mid-1950s, Dr John D. Isaacs of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography suggested towing a colossal Antarctic iceberg across the Pacific Ocean to Southern California. While the project never progressed beyond the conceptual stage, it sparked decades of scientific and engineering research into whether icebergs could one day be used as freshwater reservoirs.
